title: Sex Differences Among University Students With Autism Spectrum Disorder in Japan: The Past Diagnosis Influences Subsequent Suicidal Behavior and Career Outcomes
abstract: Background Previous studies suggest that ASD diagnosis may be delayed among female university students with relatively high IQ because of camouflaging behaviors. However, evidence from Japan remains limited. Therefore, this exploratory study examined sex differences in clinical characteristics and outcomes. Aims The study is aimed at (1) comparing comorbidities, interpersonal problems, school absences, suicidal behaviors, and postgraduation outcomes between male and female university students; and (2) examining sex differences according to the presence or absence of a prior ASD diagnosis. Methods This study was designed as an exploratory retrospective observational study. This study analyzed clinical records of 93 university students with ASD (49 males, 44 females) who attended a mental health clinic between 2013 and 2018. Comorbidities, school absences, interpersonal problems, suicidal behaviors, previous ASD diagnosis, and postgraduate career status (e.g., full‐time employment, part‐time employment, or unemployment) were compared using chi‐square tests. Results Male students had a higher rate of prior diagnosis. Depressive disorders were the most common comorbidity in both sexes. Among female students, suicidal behaviors were significantly associated with school absence. In terms of career outcomes, female students were less likely to obtain regular employment. Conclusion Female students with ASD had lower rates of prior ASD diagnosis and higher rates of multiple self‐harm behaviors than male students. Camouflaging, although not directly assessed in this study, may be one possible explanation for the lower rate of prior ASD diagnosis among female students. These findings highlight the importance of recognizing less apparent autistic characteristics and associated mental health difficulties in female university students.
